British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. Doerkson would probably be among the first to acknowledge that his route to the premiership has been anything but typical. Of the last five B.C. premiers, three were political staffers and two were lawyers, and many MLAs start their road to the provincial legislature via local politics: the MLAs-elect for the two Kamloops ridings bordering Cariboo-Chilcotin, Peter Milobar and Ward Stamer, were first the mayors of Kamloops and Barriere respectively. Doerkson’s path was considerably different, and more colourful. Born in New Westminster in 1968, he grew up in Surrey and Salmon Arm before moving to Williams Lake in 2001. items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Random draw makes Jennifer Thoss Lytton’s mayor after 45-45 tie
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Jennifer Thoss will become mayor of Lytton, British Columbia, after a random draw broke a 45-45 tie with incumbent Denise O’Connor in the Oct. 17 election. A judicial recount at Kamloops Provincial Court on Tuesday confirmed the tally before the draw selected Thoss. Thoss will lead a village rebuilding after a 2021 wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of its structures. A former councillor, she has criticized the pace of recovery and warned that more than $50 million in planned infrastructure could overwhelm Lytton’s reduced tax base. O’Connor defended the need for recovery staff and infrastructure to attract residents. Thoss said after the draw that she would focus on team-building.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] B.C. voters cast ballots in close race as officials hand-count votes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

British Columbia voters are choosing a 93-member legislature Saturday in a snap provincial election called two years early, with the governing New Democratic Party (NDP) and the Conservative Party of B.C. running close in final polls. During the campaign, Premier David Eby acknowledged frustration over the early election call, while both major parties promoted competing plans on affordability, health care and the economy. Eby initially cited U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade threat as a reason to seek a new mandate, then said he should have explained more clearly that the legislature had stalled under the NDP’s narrow majority. Eby also accused interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson of serving as a “Trojan horse” for extremists in his party; Doerkson called that characterization “absurd”. Election officials will count election-day ballots by hand because the snap vote left Elections BC too little time to prepare enough tabulators. Officials will electronically tabulate advance-voting and electoral-office ballots and report those results first. Absentee and mail-in ballots will not be included in election-night totals; they are scheduled for the final count from Nov. 6 to Nov. 10.

Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

U.S. federal AI regulation remains stalled in Congress, but a local report said the next Congress could take it up in January. The 2026-27 El Niño has strengthened across the tropical Pacific and is forecast to rank among the strongest on record, peaking during the Northern Hemisphere autumn and winter. In the United States, forecasts point to warmer-than-average temperatures, wetter conditions in parts of the West and Southwest, and less rain and snow in the Pacific Northwest. California has already seen unusually high coastal water levels; a UC Davis report identifies low-lying roads, airports and neighborhoods at risk of flooding if high tides and winter storms coincide. Former officials and scientists warn that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has lost roughly one-fifth of its staff since January 2025, weakening its forecasting and response capacity ahead of the season. New Zealand’s outlook for November 2026 through January 2027 points to a greater likelihood of dry conditions in the north and east of the North Island and heavier rain in the south and west of the South Island.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] Spain train crash kills 68 as investigators probe control error
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A Renfe high-speed train struck a stationary Iryo train near Urda in central Spain on Oct. 28, killing at least 68 people and injuring 107, including 15 in serious condition. The two trains, travelling from Madrid toward Seville, carried a total of 544 passengers. It was Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail crash this year, following a January collision near Adamuz that killed 46. Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure disabled the LZB safety system on a 63-kilometre stretch at about 8:30 a.m., stopping six trains. He said Madrid’s control centre then authorized the Renfe train to resume at normal speed; it travelled about 25 kilometres before hitting the stopped Iryo train at 8:53 a.m. Puente called the instruction “inexplicable” and said the drivers were not at fault. Iryo said its train had not been authorized to restart and remained stopped after the signal failure, according to ABC News Australia. Investigators are examining the differing accounts. Spain declared three days of national mourning, from Oct. 29 through 31. The Rail Accident Investigation Commission and judicial authorities are investigating. Rail services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended.

items.title: [news.climate.columbia.edu] Study finds human-caused warming reversed early North American glaciation
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A study published in Science says the Barnes Ice Cap on Canada’s Baffin Island, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began expanding about 2,000 years ago. Researchers identify that growth as the start of a new glacial period. The ice began retreating around 1960 as summer warming caused it to lose more ice than it gained. The team reconstructed the ice cap’s history using vegetation preserved beneath the ice and dates from exposed rocks. The researchers define the start of a glacial period as the resumption of ice-sheet growth, differing from models that place the next glaciation thousands or tens of thousands of years in the future. Models cited by the researchers project that the Barnes Ice Cap could disappear within the next few centuries. The researchers say rising atmospheric carbon dioxide makes a return to glacial conditions extremely unlikely.

In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.

Legombang Treehouse reinterprets traditional Balinese architecture as a contemporary tropical family home, using reclaimed timber, passive design, and a treehouse-like structure woven around the site's existing trees. Designed by Cave Urban co-founder Jed Long for his own family, the house is located in Pantai Lembeng, Ketewel, Bali. As both architect and client, Jed had the opportunity to explore his own approach to tropical family living without the constraints of a conventional client brief.
